raw_case_text:
A 69-year-old man was admitted due to fever, chills and lassitude from 4 days ago. He was well until 4 days ago when fever developed in the last day of his trip to Southeast Asia (Malaysia and Thailand). Then, he traveled to Dubai and after three days with fever and chills, he developed malaise, lassitude and sweating. He was seen in a hospital and after primary care discharged with Amoxicillin-Clavulanic acid. During flight to Tehran, he was lethargic and after arrival, he was immediately transferred to a hospital.
On admission, he was febrile (body temperature: 39.5 C) with tachycardia, tachypnea, and normal blood pressure. Other his physical examinations revealed no abnormality, except for fine scars of healed abrasions related to walking on a beach on his first day in Thailand (Figure 1).
The patient had diabetes mellitus and hypertension since eleven years ago, and also nasal polyps and sleep disorder. His medications included diltiazem and glibenclamide. He was neither a drinker nor a smoker and did not use any illicit drugs. Allergic history was unremarkable.
Laboratory analysis showed leukocytosis (17,000/ ml)with a shift to the left, normal renal and liver function tests, with 470 mg/dl random glucose level, ESR 42mm/hr and LDH 630 mg/dl. Repeated cardiac markers including creatinine kinase-MB and troponin I were within the normal ranges. Peripheral blood smear was negative for malaria.
Chest X-ray (CXR) was obtained (Figure 2). Based on roentgenographic findings (Figures 2 and 3), ceftriaxone and azithromycin were initiated. But the day after, the patient was transferred to cardiac care unit due to new left bundle branch block and hypokinesia in echocardiography.
A few hours later, ventricular tachycardia resulted in hypotension; and the patient was complicated with acute tubular necrosis. White blood cell counts rose up to 22,000/ml and 18% band cells. New portable CXR and CT scan revealed more diffuse and extensive alveolar infiltrations (Figures 4 and 5).
The patient was intubated and vancomycin, ciprofloxacin and meropenem were started. Amphotericin B was initiated for one day and then changed to voriconazole; as vancomycin to linezolid. The day after, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) was added to the regimen.
Bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) were performed. Blood and BAL cultures revealed heavy growth of Burkholderia pseudomallei.
According to the aforementioned culture results, the patient was treated with meropenem and TMP-SMX, while other antibiotics were discontinued.
Fortunately, after 3 weeks, the patient was discharged with stable status and normal pulmonary function; and eradication therapy with TMP-SMX continued for about 3 months. The control lung CT scan after one month demonstrated significant improvement (Figure 6).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 69-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of fever, chills, malaise, sweating, and lethargy following recent travel to Southeast Asia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was well until 4 days prior to admission when he developed fever on the last day of a trip to Malaysia and Thailand, where he had sustained minor foot abrasions while walking on a beach on his first day in Thailand. He then traveled to Dubai and experienced 3 days of fever, chills, malaise, lassitude, and sweating; he was evaluated at a local hospital and discharged on oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid. During his flight to Tehran, he became progressively lethargic and was transferred directly to our hospital upon arrival.
subjective.past_medical_history: 11-year history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension, as well as nasal polyps and a sleep disorder. Non-smoker, non-drinker, and denied illicit drug use. Recent travel history to Malaysia, Thailand, and Dubai.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, malaise, lassitude, sweating, and lethargy. Home medications included diltiazem and glibenclamide. No known allergies.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, he was febrile (body temperature 39.5 C), tachycardic, and tachypneic with normal blood pressure. Skin examination showed fine scars of healed abrasions on his foot/leg from walking on a beach in Thailand; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (WBC 17,000/mL with a left shift), random blood glucose 470 mg/dL, ESR 42 mm/hr, LDH 630 mg/dL, normal renal and liver function tests, normal serial cardiac biomarkers (CK-MB and troponin I), and negative peripheral blood smear for malaria. Initial chest X-ray showed pulmonary infiltrates. On hospital day 2, ECG and echocardiography revealed a new left bundle branch block and myocardial hypokinesia, followed by ventricular tachycardia, hypotension, acute tubular necrosis, and worsening leukocytosis (WBC 22,000/mL with 18% band cells) with diffuse bilateral alveolar infiltrations on portable chest X-ray.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic CT scans demonstrated extensive, diffuse bilateral alveolar infiltrations. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed for microbiological sampling.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Acute severe pneumonic and septicemic melioidosis complicated by cardiac conduction abnormality (left bundle branch block), ventricular tachycardia, septic/cardiogenic hypotension, and acute tubular necrosis, confirmed by heavy growth of Burkholderia pseudomallei in both blood and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) cultures. Management and clinical course: Empiric ceftriaxone and azithromycin were initially started, followed by ICU transfer, endotracheal intubation, and broad-spectrum escalation (vancomycin switched to linezolid, ciprofloxacin, meropenem, amphotericin B switched to voriconazole, and addition of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole). Once B. pseudomallei was confirmed, other antimicrobials were discontinued and targeted therapy was continued with intravenous meropenem plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX). He was discharged in stable condition with normal pulmonary function after 3 weeks of inpatient therapy, completed ~3 months of oral TMP-SMX eradication therapy, and showed marked radiographic resolution on 1-month follow-up chest CT.
